Here's some pointers about getting a rifle:

- Get a Wylde .223 barrel. It can handle either .223 REM or 5.55 NATO

- Make sure the lower is stamped "multi" caliber. If it is stamped 5.56 and you use .223 you can technically get in trouble.

- Standard barrel length is 16". They can come longer or sorter. 12"-14.5" is considered an SBR, which requires a special license. 7.5"-10.5" is considered pistol length. Pistol AR15s are very popular, but there are some limitations, such as: you have to use a brace instead of a stock, and you cannot use a vertical grip. Doing otherwise will make your gun an illegal firearm.

- Get an M-Lok guard rail. Keymod has a lot of negatives, so stray away from it. Picatinny mods can be put on M-Lok easily.

I built my rifles and bought parts from PSA, Anderson, Aero, Ceratec, and Davidson Defense. I haven't had issues with any of my parts. If you can wait, all these places have sales where you can save up to $200 bucks.

If you do plan on building your own rifle, nearly all AR15 parts are compatible across manufactures. Get your completed lower fro Anderson for $50, then get your other parts from any of the sites I mentioned. Gun shows sell parts at good prices.

If you want to buy a completed AR15, $600 is the average price. You can find a complete gun for $400, but I'd be worried about quality. In my opinion, you can find a better gun than the one you posted but for the same price.

As far as hand guns:

- Revolvers are less prone to jam and have a barrel is fixed, meaning that they are more reliable and accurate. However, you are limited to the 5-7 shots.

- Pistols commonly hold 7-17 rounds.

- The heavier the gun, the more recoil it absorbs when you shoot it

- Polymer pistols are taking over. They are very sturdy, light weight, and much cheaper than their metal counter-parts. Police departments and military branches are opting for polymer because of this.

There are some pros/cons for either polymer or metal. For hand guns, like I said before, weight matters. The heavier the gun, the more recoil it will absorb; meaning, you will feel less recoil. Polymer guns are lighter, so you will feel more recoil when shooting them. Given that they weigh less, it makes conceal carry easier. Polymer handguns are usually much cheaper than their metal counterparts too.

There are polymer lowers for AR15, but the weight difference is unnoticeable. There is almost no price difference between a polymer and metal lower, so I would just get metal.

For caliber .380 is fine. There are a lot of people that say "I don't do anything smaller than .45 ACP". They are simply misinformed. Muzzle velocity is more important than caliber when it comes to stopping power. The .38 special and .357 Mag are smaller than the .45, but studies show that they can out-perform it. Keep in mind, .380 is the smallest caliber recommended for ccw. I prefer 9mm due to its wide availability and affordability.

A lot of good info already, but I'd just like to put in my opinion, as I've owned and sold a lot of guns.

Regarding the comments on poly pistols; There's nothing wrong with them, it's simply that plastic is weaker than alloy. If you drop the fucker, your house catches on fire... Whatever, you never know; it can get damaged more easily.

With that said, I currently carry an M&P Shield .40 Cal.

I prefer metal firearms... I'll just carry something for a while, resell it, get something else. I guess it all depends on your priorities. I carry the M&P because it's a single-stack, it's light, and it's a great round. It's essentially the same amount of rounds as a 1911, but with a faster bullet, more compact, and much lighter.

If it's something just to keep around the house, I would prefer something a bit more stout.

Your location effects what you can carry, as well. Hard to carry a big, metal gun in a tropical climate.

As for the rifle, ARs are great, but I also recommend checking out a Mini- (AKA, a Ruger Ranch Rifle). Essentially, the same thing, same caliber, same amount of modification options. What one needs to keep in mind is the possibility of actually having to use the thing. You can make either look like a "big, scary, tactical semi-automatic assault gun." It's easier to make a Mini-14 look like an average hunting rifle.
